The Contracting Officer may at any time, by written order, and without notice to the sureties, if any, make changes within the general scope of this contract in any one or more of the following: a. Method of shipment or packing. b. Place of delivery. c. Time of delivery. If any such change causes an increase or decrease in the cost of, or the time required for, performance of any part of the work under this contract, whether or not changed by the order, the Contracting Officer shall make an equitable adjustment in the contract price, the delivery schedule, or both, and shall modify the contract, unless the contract terms provide for regional delivery pricing that covers cost adjustments. The Contractor must assert its right to an adjustment under this clause within 30 days from the date of receipt of the written order. However, if the Contracting Officer decides that the facts justify it, the Contracting Officer may receive and act upon a proposal submitted before final payment of the contract. If the Contractor’s proposal includes the cost of property made obsolete or excess by the change, the Contracting Officer shall have the right to prescribe the manner of the disposition of the property. Failure to agree to any adjustment shall be a dispute under the Disputes clause. However, nothing in this clause shall excuse the Contractor from proceeding with the contract as changed. The optical frequency combs (OFCs) that underpin photonic microwave oscillators are key components in multiple other record-setting optical technologies. Optical clocks developed for position, navigation, and timing (PNT) applications employ OFCs to stabilize RF frequencies to atomic references with extreme precision over timescales of hours and beyond. While the realization of compact and rugged optical clocks for tactical military platforms remains an outstanding goal, it may be possible to significantly simplify the design of optical clocks for stability over the comparably shorter timescales of RF applications ranging from seconds to tens of seconds. In this regime, OFCs are likely to be the leading contributor of size, weight, and power, and chip-scale implementations could enable their proliferation and deployment. Dual-comb techniques of time transfer further enable such stability to be distributed over long distances

The Proposer must request the CUI Addendum by the deadline stated in the Overview section. A. Background The performance of best-in-class microwave sources fielded today, such as oven-controlled crystal oscillators (OCXO) and surface- or bulk-acoustic wave (SAW/BAW) oscillators, degrades by many orders of magnitude when subjected to challenging ambient conditions, particularly vibration. External acoustics naturally couple into the 10–100 MHz mechanical modes that OCXOs transduce into electrical outputs. Electronic multiplication stages further multiply vibration-induced noise by a factor of ~10 6 when converting to the gigahertz regime of interest for high-resolution radar and high-bandwidth electronic warfare (EW) and communications. Conventional approaches to mitigate vibration effects employ bootstrapping of multiple oscillators, active feedback, and mechanical damping or isolation, but applying these solutions requires significant added size, weight, and/or power that are not compatible with the constraints of compact, highly mobile platforms. As a result, the RF system architectures that deploy to the edge are unable to employ

ignificantly simplify the design of optical clocks for stability over the comparably shorter timescales of RF applications ranging from seconds to tens of seconds. In this regime, OFCs are likely to be the leading contributor of size, weight, and power, and chip-scale implementations could enable their proliferation and deployment. Dual-comb techniques of time transfer further enable such stability to be distributed over long distances across a platform or between physically remote RF nodes via fiber or free-space laser links. Additional implementation of OFCs for multi-wavelength communication channels offers a path to send vast data volumes over distance. DARPA’s Photonics in the Package for Extreme Scalability (PIPES) program, launched in 2019, showed that integrated photonic OFC transceivers could be co-packaged with the advanced microelectronics needed for broadband RF systems 4,5,6. Collectively, chip-scale OFCs offer multiple breakthrough functionalities to generate and distribute pure frequencies, stable time, and high- bandwidth data across and between RF systems, with the potential for novel architectures that exploit such performance to overcome performance bottlenecks inherited from electronic timing and communication standards. 1 Nakamura, T., Groman, W., Ji, Q

obile defense platforms. The program will also study the utility of additional optical device functionality such as time transfer and high-bandwidth data movement based on proposer-identified use cases. The program will rapidly develop the required componentry and system architectures necessary to take advantage of the optical timing backbone, culminating in an on-platform demonstration. At the component level, the program aims to demonstrate photonic microwave oscillators with: Phase noise < -120 dBc/Hz at 100 Hz offset 7, Phase noise < -150 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz offset, Relative timing error < 1 picosecond for 1–100 second intervals, and Volume < 300 cc. While RAAPTR is specifically seeking photonic approaches to microwave generation, DARPA is open to any concept that achieves program metrics. Integrated photonics, micro-optics, and/or other chip-scale photonic device approaches are not required; however, proposals for fiber-optic solutions will be closely scrutinized during proposal review for concepts that enable overcoming their susceptibility to ambient acoustic noise. At the system architecture level, RAAPTR aims to demonstrate not only the optical components necessary for such a backbone, but also the ancillary analog-RF and digital-RF capacity sufficient to maintain the

The optical frequency combs (OFCs) that underpin photonic microwave oscillators are key components in multiple other record-setting optical technologies. Optical clocks developed for position, navigation, and timing (PNT) applications employ OFCs to stabilize RF frequencies to atomic references with extreme precision over timescales of hours and beyond. While the realization of compact and rugged optical clocks for tactical military platforms remains an outstanding goal, it may be possible to significantly simplify the design of optical clocks for stability over the comparably shorter timescales of RF applications ranging from seconds to tens of seconds. In this regime, OFCs are likely to be the leading contributor of size, weight, and power, and chip-scale implementations could enable their proliferation and deployment. Dual-comb techniques of time transfer further enable such stability to be distributed over long distances

The Proposer must request the CUI Addendum by the deadline stated in the Overview section. A. Background The performance of best-in-class microwave sources fielded today, such as oven-controlled crystal oscillators (OCXO) and surface- or bulk-acoustic wave (SAW/BAW) oscillators, degrades by many orders of magnitude when subjected to challenging ambient conditions, particularly vibration. External acoustics naturally couple into the 10–100 MHz mechanical modes that OCXOs transduce into electrical outputs. Electronic multiplication stages further multiply vibration-induced noise by a factor of ~10 6 when converting to the gigahertz regime of interest for high-resolution radar and high-bandwidth electronic warfare (EW) and communications. Conventional approaches to mitigate vibration effects employ bootstrapping of multiple oscillators, active feedback, and mechanical damping or isolation, but applying these solutions requires significant added size, weight, and/or power that are not compatible with the constraints of compact, highly mobile platforms. As a result, the RF system architectures that deploy to the edge are unable to employ

ignificantly simplify the design of optical clocks for stability over the comparably shorter timescales of RF applications ranging from seconds to tens of seconds. In this regime, OFCs are likely to be the leading contributor of size, weight, and power, and chip-scale implementations could enable their proliferation and deployment. Dual-comb techniques of time transfer further enable such stability to be distributed over long distances across a platform or between physically remote RF nodes via fiber or free-space laser links. Additional implementation of OFCs for multi-wavelength communication channels offers a path to send vast data volumes over distance. DARPA’s Photonics in the Package for Extreme Scalability (PIPES) program, launched in 2019, showed that integrated photonic OFC transceivers could be co-packaged with the advanced microelectronics needed for broadband RF systems 4,5,6. Collectively, chip-scale OFCs offer multiple breakthrough functionalities to generate and distribute pure frequencies, stable time, and high- bandwidth data across and between RF systems, with the potential for novel architectures that exploit such performance to overcome performance bottlenecks inherited from electronic timing and communication standards. 1 Nakamura, T., Groman, W., Ji, Q

obile defense platforms. The program will also study the utility of additional optical device functionality such as time transfer and high-bandwidth data movement based on proposer-identified use cases. The program will rapidly develop the required componentry and system architectures necessary to take advantage of the optical timing backbone, culminating in an on-platform demonstration. At the component level, the program aims to demonstrate photonic microwave oscillators with: Phase noise < -120 dBc/Hz at 100 Hz offset 7, Phase noise < -150 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz offset, Relative timing error < 1 picosecond for 1–100 second intervals, and Volume < 300 cc. While RAAPTR is specifically seeking photonic approaches to microwave generation, DARPA is open to any concept that achieves program metrics. Integrated photonics, micro-optics, and/or other chip-scale photonic device approaches are not required; however, proposals for fiber-optic solutions will be closely scrutinized during proposal review for concepts that enable overcoming their susceptibility to ambient acoustic noise. At the system architecture level, RAAPTR aims to demonstrate not only the optical components necessary for such a backbone, but also the ancillary analog-RF and digital-RF capacity sufficient to maintain the
